title: Kernel panic timeline sleuth & mitigation playbook
content:
Purpose:
This note is a compact on-call + lab playbook to stitch together kernel panic events that correlate with GPU ECC spikes, NVLink negotiation flaps, and occasional driver-level stack traces. It is intentionally operational: quick commands, timeline-alignment heuristics, quarantine/rollback options, and lab repro experiments.

Scope / when to use:
- Repeated kernel panics across a rack or subset of nodes where initial signs point to GPU subsystem (ECC counters, nvidia-driver oops, PCIe resets).
- Intermittent single-node panics that recover after node reboot but recur under similar workload shapes.
- Cases where NVLink retraining or link flaps in logs coincide with dmesg OOPS or GPU hangs.

High-level hypothesis patterns (working list):
- Pattern A: Burst of correctable ECC errors immediately preceding driver hang + kernel stacktrace referencing nvidia. This suggests either marginal memory (thermal/voltage) or a firmware regression that exposes a rare ECC handling bug.
- Pattern B: NVLink negotiation failures (link training retries) correlated with internal link reset messages in kernel logs and subsequent GPU eviction. Often shows as a small cluster across GPUs on same NVLink fabric.
- Pattern C: PCIe reset cascade where GPU driver triggers a controller reset, baskets of GPUs re-enumerate, and the kernel hits a panic due to IO starvation in a tight critical section.
- Pattern D: Timing drift between kernel/driver logs and user-level telemetry (Prometheus) causing misaligned correlation — must do careful timestamp alignment.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Preserve the node (do not reboot if you need core/dmesg) — if alive, run:
   - sudo dmesg -T | tail -n 200 > /tmp/dmesg-tmp.log
   - sudo journalctl -k -b -1 -o short-precise | sed -n '1,500p' > /tmp/journal-prev-boot.log
2) Collect GPU counters and driver status (if nvidia-smi works):
   - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,driver_version,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 -f /tmp/nvidia-smi-snapshot.csv --loop-count=3
   - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=ecc.errors.corrected.volatile,ecc.errors.uncorrected.volatile --format=csv >> /tmp/ecc-counters.csv
3) Grep for obvious signs:
   - grep -iE "nvidia|nvlink|nvlink.*training|ecc|timeout|gpu hang|GPU has fallen off the bus|PCI:.*reset" /tmp/dmesg-tmp.log /tmp/journal-prev-boot.log
4) If kernel panic already happened and node rebooted: collect oldest journal entries and previous dmesg (-1 boot). Use timestamps to correlate with Prometheus traces.
5) Snapshot nvlink state (if nvidia-smi supports):
   - nvidia-smi nvlink --showtopo (or nvlink --status) and save output.
6) Note uptime, last reboot cause, and running pods/containers on node. Export kubelet logs for that timeframe.

Timeline alignment heuristics:
- Convert all timestamps to UTC and align to the most precise source: kernel dmesg/journalctl (-o short-iso/precise).
- If Prometheus metrics are coarse (1m scrape), check local telemetry (node_exporter with 15s) or the app-level timestamps.
- Sequence to correlate: ECC counter surge -> nvlink retrain messages -> driver stack -> PCIe reset -> kernel OOPS/panic. If this sequence is observed consistently, treat it as causal order.
- Watch for small time deltas (<30s) between ECC increments and driver errors. If ECC increments are minutes earlier, they may be background noise.

Commands & useful one-liners (copy/paste):
- Dump kernel and driver traces: sudo dmesg -T | sed -n '1,500p' > /tmp/dmesg-head.log; sudo journalctl -k -b -1 -o short-precise > /tmp/prev-kernel.log
- ECC counters history (if DCGM available): dcgmi dmon -e --iterations 3 --delay 1 > /tmp/dcgmi-dmon.log
- Search for NVLink training failures: sudo grep -i "training" /var/log/messages /var/log/kern.log /var/log/syslog || true
- Capture stack traces from crash dumps (if we have driver crash dumps configured): sudo find /var/crash -type f -mtime -7 -ls

On-call mitigation playbook (fast, reversible):
1) Soft quarantine: cordon node in k8s and drain non-critical pods. Move heavy inference work off the node.
   - kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=60
2) Disable NVLink on the node as a test (if hardware/OS supports safe toggling) to see if panics stop. Document steps for hardware team.
3) If ECC counts are rapidly increasing, schedule immediate reboot for hardware isolation and escalate to HW team for ECC scrub / power-cycling PSU.
4) Firmware/driver quick rollback: if driver upgrade was recent and multiple nodes show the same symptoms, rollback driver to last known-good (document driver version). Use canary nodes via rolling rollback.
5) If panic is reproducible in lab, consider enabling driver debug logs and increasing ECC scrub frequency temporarily.

Lab repro protocol (safe, isolated):
- Goal: reproduce panic within controlled environment and capture full kernel+driver trace.
1) Select equivalent hardware with same BIOS and firmware. Snapshot current firmware/driver versions.
2) Use a stress pattern that historically triggered the issue: mixture of small (<512 token) low-latency chat workloads plus periodic long context batches to saturate KV cache. Alternatively, a synthetic memory torture test (memtest-like) combined with frequent nvlink transfers between GPUs (cudaPeerAccess copy patterns).
3) Run with driver debug enabled (dmesg verbosity up, nvidia.quirks if available) and serial console attached.
4) If NVLink suspected, enable and disable NVLink programmatically across GPUs and watch for link retrain messages.
5) Keep steady telemetry: high-frequency sampling of ECC counters, PCIe reset counts, and temperature probes.

When to escalate to firmware/hardware vendor:
- Persistent uncorrected ECC errors on a GPU or group of GPUs after power-cycle and scrub.
- NVLink retrains present across multiple identical nodes in the same rack (fabric-level problem).
- Driver stack trace shows internal kernel calls into vendor-specific modules with no clear mitigation.

Post-incident runbook items (post triage):
- Collect and attach: dmesg, journalctl kernels (-b -1), nvidia-smi snapshots, dcgmi logs, ipmi logs, BIOS/firmware versions, kubelet logs, and list of pods at time-of-event.
- Create JIRA incident ticket with: timeline, nodes affected, recovered/not recovered, actions taken, and hypothesis. Tag with SRE/infra/firmware.
- If hardware vendor engaged, include serial numbers, full logs, and reproducible lab steps.
- Add a lightweight automated detection alert: if ECC.corrected.volatile increases by >X in 1m for any GPU AND nvlink retrain count > 0, fire a high-priority SRE alert and recommend cordon.

Open questions / investigation threads (to surface in follow-ups):
- Are ECC surges correlated with specific workload shards or particular model sizes? (tracking: model IDs, batch sizes).
- Does ambient temperature correlate with ECC bursts? Should we test with artificially raised rack inlet temps?
- Is there an interaction with particular BIOS power-management modes? A/B test power management profiles in lab.

Owner & contact during incidents:
- Primary oncall SRE: Maya Chen (this doc owner)
- Backup: Arjun Patel, Sofia Martinez
- Hardware escalation: Noah Blake (HW liaison)
- Slack channel: #sre-gpu (use thread prefix "GPU-PANIC:")

Follow-up artifacts to produce after stabilization:
- Postmortem draft within 72h with timeline and root-cause hypothesis status.
- Lab report containing reproducible steps or confirmed non-reproducibility.
- Action items: alert rule, sprint ticket for driver pin/rollback strategy, rack-level cooling check, scheduling maintenance window if firmware update required.

Notes to self (informal scratch):
- If you see "GPU has fallen off the bus" and a subsequent pci bus reset, don't assume fix by reboot; look for PCIe link flaps first.
- When in doubt on timestamps, rely on serial console (no clock drift) and attach NTP status to every capture.
- Keep a small set of canary nodes with older stable driver pinned for quick rollback and test deploys.

Last updated: 2028-10-02 by Maya Chen.
